children: NASA announced a series of contracts and mission plans Saturday to expand its lunar exploration program, including a $10 billion commercial delivery framework, a nuclear-powered rover and new transportation and communications systems to support a permanent base near the Moon’s South Pole.

The announcements, made Saturday at an aerospace exhibition at Kennedy Space Center in Florida, outline NASA’s strategy for developing lunar infrastructure through partnerships with commercial space companies, including Blue Origin (
), SpaceX
, Lockheed Martin
and Northrop Grumman

For investors, the awards signal a growing market for commercial space transportation, robotics, communications and power systems. NASA’s approach creates opportunities for established aerospace contractors and smaller space technology companies, although the full value of the contracting frameworks isn't guaranteed revenue. Future orders will depend on funding, competitive selections and mission requirements.

Under its Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative, NASA selected eight companies eligible to compete for lunar cargo delivery missions over the next decade. The companies are Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace
, Intuitive Machines
, ispace-U.S., Lockheed Martin Space, Northrop Grumman Space Systems, SpaceX and Voyager Technologies

The new CLPS 2 contracting framework has a combined ceiling of $10 billion over 10 years. NASA also increased the maximum value of its existing CLPS contract to $4.2 billion from $2.6 billion to support early lunar base development. The original program will remain active through November 2028, with additional time to complete deliveries already awarded.

NASA separately awarded Blue Origin a $94 million contract to deliver a nuclear-powered robotic rover called PROMISE to the lunar South Pole, with a potential additional $140 million tied to performance. The six-wheeled vehicle will investigate underground ice deposits, analyze lunar soil and collect information needed to select landing sites and develop infrastructure.

The agency's Jet Propulsion Laboratory will build PROMISE using spare components and engineering models from its Mars rover programs. NASA is targeting a late-2028 launch and an 18-month mission. Nuclear power will allow the vehicle to operate during extended lunar nights and in permanently shadowed areas where water ice may exist.

NASA also awarded six task orders totaling approximately $1.3 billion to Arrow Science and Technology, Blue Origin and Impulse Space for launch and orbital transportation services. The contracts cover missions involving communications, navigation, robotic reconnaissance and the movement of cargo between Earth orbit and the Moon.

The transportation awards fall under NASA’s Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare program, which has an overall contracting ceiling of $5 billion. Planned missions will use rockets including Blue Origin’s New Glenn, Relativity Space’s Terran R and SpaceX’s Falcon 9, while several commercial providers will supply spacecraft for transportation between orbits.

Among the planned missions are MoonFall robotic drones designed to survey terrain that conventional rovers cannot easily reach. NASA also intends to test orbital transfer vehicles capable of moving cargo toward the Moon, potentially increasing the amount of equipment that future lunar landers can deliver.

SpaceX received a separate assignment under an existing lunar logistics contract to deploy communications satellites using its Starship spacecraft in 2028. The demonstration will test technology intended to maintain communications among astronauts, ground controllers and lunar installations.
NASA also selected Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, Redwire

and privately held Yank Technologies to supply components for a small lunar power and communications tower. The project will combine solar generation, battery storage and wireless power transfer. NASA expects to seek proposals for larger integrated power systems in early 2027.

The investments are part of NASA’s broader effort to establish a sustained human presence on the Moon before pursuing crewed missions to Mars. The agency plans to develop the lunar base through successive robotic and human missions, allowing infrastructure to be tested and expanded as additional capabilities become available.
